paragraphs.heading: Fool's gold
paragraphs.text: Pyrite, also called iron pyrite, is an iron sulfide with the chemical formula FeS₂. It is the most abundant sulfide mineral. Its metallic luster and pale brass-yellow colour make it look a little like gold on the surface, and that is where the nickname fool's gold comes from.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is found
paragraphs.text: Pyrite usually occurs together with other sulfides or oxides. It turns up in quartz veins, in sedimentary and metamorphic rock, in beds of coal, and in fossils as a replacement mineral. Despite the nickname, pyrite is sometimes found along with small quantities of real gold. A substantial part of that gold is "invisible gold" built into the pyrite itself. As of 1997, the chemical state of this gold was still controversial.

paragraphs.heading: The stone that strikes fire
paragraphs.text: The name pyrite comes from a Greek phrase meaning a stone or mineral which strikes fire, built on the Greek word for fire. The oldest definitive evidence of fire making comes from a Neanderthal site in Suffolk, England, and is about 400,000 years old. Burnt soil was found there, along with flint handaxes cracked by fire and two pieces of iron pyrite, which was used with flint to strike sparks. Ötzi, a well-preserved natural mummy, was a man of the Ötztal Alps who lived between 3350 and 3105 BCE. He carried tinder fungus, flint and pyrite for making sparks.

paragraphs.heading: A source of acid
paragraphs.text: Since classical times pyrite has been used to make copperas, which is ferrous sulfate. Iron pyrite was piled into heaps and left to weather. Acidic liquid ran off the heap, and this was then boiled with iron to give iron sulfate. In the 15th century, new leaching methods of this kind began to replace burning sulfur as a source of sulfuric acid, and by the 19th century leaching had become the dominant method. Pyrite is still used commercially to produce sulfur dioxide, for uses such as the paper industry, and to make sulfuric acid.

paragraphs.heading: Guns, jewellery and radios
paragraphs.text: In the 16th and 17th centuries pyrite was briefly popular as a source of ignition in early firearms. The best-known case is the wheellock, in which a piece of pyrite was held against a circular file to strike the sparks that fired the gun. Small faceted pieces of pyrite, often set in silver, have been made into what is called marcasite jewelry since ancient times. In the early years of the 20th century, pyrite served as a mineral detector in radio receivers, and crystal radio hobbyists still use it.

paragraphs.heading: Batteries and solar panels
paragraphs.text: A newer commercial use of pyrite is as the cathode material in Energizer brand lithium metal batteries of the non-rechargeable kind. Pyrite is also a semiconductor. It absorbs visible light strongly, and for that reason it has been proposed as an abundant, non-toxic and inexpensive material for low-cost photovoltaic solar panels. More recent efforts aim at thin-film solar cells made entirely of pyrite.
